description: Width tiers for ACARA v9 Geography Year 9. Covers the Biomes and Interconnections topic groupings (K01–K08) and geographical inquiry skills (S01–S06). K-strand uses phenomena_contexts; S-strand uses task_contexts.
subject: Geography

width_notes.minimum_width: The narrowest honest engagement that satisfies the descriptor's command term. For K-strand descriptors: the fewest phenomena or contexts that still genuinely meet the command term (identify, explain, examine). For S-strand descriptors: the narrowest task context in which the skill is demonstrably practised. Minimum is not what is easy — it is what is non-negotiable.
width_notes.typical_width: Full descriptor scope as ACARA intended, grounded in the most common elaboration cases. For K-strand: covers the representative phenomena and comparisons the descriptor specifies (including Australia and a country in Asia where indicated). For S-strand: covers the range of task types across the inquiry topics the standard supports.
width_notes.wider: Enrichment directions that add new phenomena, contexts or task types — not harder versions of the same context. For K-strand: additional biome types, cross-cultural cases, First Nations knowledge directions, or scale extensions. For S-strand: application of the skill in novel task contexts, complex data types, or methodological reflection tasks.
width_notes.elaborations: ACARA elaborations are treated as source data, not a checklist. Typical_width is grounded in the most common elaboration cases. Wider may infer beyond elaborations where clearly within the descriptor's territory and year band. First Nations elaborations are always represented in wider.

AC9HG9K01.minimum_width: Identify at least five major terrestrial biomes and describe their distinctive climate, soil and vegetation characteristics; locate them on a world map and identify which are present in Australia.
AC9HG9K01.typical_width: Identify and describe the major aquatic and terrestrial biomes of Australia and at least one country in Asia, mapping their distribution; interpret and explain patterns and trends in biome productivity comparing Australia with an Asian country; explain how interconnections between environmental processes (atmosphere, hydrosphere, lithosphere, biosphere) and at least two human activities (e.g. deforestation, mining, agriculture) alter biome characteristics.
wider: Investigate the productivity of aquatic biomes (freshwater, marine, estuarine) alongside terrestrial biomes — compare what drives productivity differences across both biome types
Examine how First Nations Australians' land management practices (e.g. cultural burning) work with biome interconnections rather than disrupting them — contrast with post-colonial land use changes
Analyse biome distribution maps across time periods to identify shifts attributable to climate change — explain what environmental process changes drive the shifts
Investigate how soil formation processes link to climate and vegetation in contrasting biomes — examine a case from a tropical and a dryland Australian biome
elaborations: identifying and describing the major aquatic and terrestrial biomes of Australia and other areas of the world, and mapping their distribution
interpreting and explaining patterns and trends in the productivity of the major aquatic and terrestrial biomes in Australia compared with a country in Asia

explaining the effects of interconnections between environmental processes (atmosphere, hydrosphere, lithosphere and biosphere) and human activities, such as deforestation, mining and agriculture on the characteristics of biomes

AC9HG9K02.minimum_width: Identify at least two biomes in Australia and one in an Asian country that produce food or non-food products; explain at least one difference between natural and agricultural ecosystems in nutrient flows or biodiversity.
AC9HG9K02.typical_width: Identify biomes in Australia and a country in Asia that produce foods and plant material; explain differences between natural and agricultural ecosystems in flows of nutrients and water and in biodiversity using the tropical rainforest biome in Indonesia as a case; explain how at least three agricultural innovations (e.g. drip irrigation, fertilisers, pesticides, GM seeds, terracing, erosion control) have increased agricultural productivity in Australia and an Asian country.
wider: Trace a specific product (e.g. palm oil, rice, wool) from biome to consumer — identify all biome types involved across the supply chain and the ecological transitions at each stage

Investigate how agroforestry and intercropping systems attempt to restore natural ecosystem functions while maintaining production — evaluate how well they succeed using nutrient flow and biodiversity evidence
Examine how First Nations Australians used multiple biomes to sustainably source food and materials — compare the ecological logic of this approach with contemporary monoculture production systems
Analyse agrobiotics as an innovation that works with biome biology rather than overriding it — compare its ecological footprint with chemical input alternatives
elaborations: identifying the biomes in Australia and a country in Asia that produce some of the foods and plant material people consume

explaining the differences between natural and agricultural ecosystems in flows of nutrients and water, and in biodiversity; for example, the tropical rainforest biome in Indonesia produces food such as fruit, grains, nuts, vegetables and spices, and non-food products such as wood, rubber, coffee, chocolate and palm oil

explaining how human alteration of biomes (for example, drip irrigation, fertilisers, pesticides, genetically modified seeds, agrobiotics, terracing, and controlling erosion and overgrazing) has increased agricultural productivity in Australia and a country in Asia

AC9HG9K03.minimum_width: Identify at least two environmental factors and at least two economic or technological factors affecting agricultural production; explain how each affects productivity in Australia or an Asian country.
AC9HG9K03.typical_width: Examine how environmental factors (climate, soil, landform, water, hazards) support higher production of staple crops such as wheat, rice and maize in Australia and an Asian country; examine how economic factors (land, labour, finance, enterprise) and technological factors (biotechnology, GIS) affect production in Australia and an Asian country; examine how agricultural innovations have reduced environmental limitations; explain the impact of interconnections between all three factor types on the yield of a specific crop in Australia.
wider: Compare how environmental factors operate differently for rice production in a monsoon climate (Asia) versus wheat production in a semi-arid climate (Australia) — explain the different constraint profiles each crop faces
Analyse how GIS technology changes farm management decisions — explain what spatial data enables that traditional farm management cannot, using a specific Australian or Asian agricultural case
Investigate how access to finance and enterprise support differs between small-scale Asian farmers and large-scale Australian commercial farmers — explain the impact on technology adoption and yield
Construct a systems diagram showing interconnections between at least three factors affecting a specific crop yield in Australia — identify at least two feedback loops
elaborations: examining how environmental factors, such as climate, soil, landform, water and hazards, support higher agricultural production, such as wheat, rice and maize, in Australia and a country in Asia

examining how economic factors such as available land, labour, finance and enterprise, and technological factors such as biotechnology and use of Geographical Information Systems (GIS) software, affect agricultural production in Australia and a country in Asia; for example, increased labour supply or access to storage, transportation and markets

examining how agricultural innovations have reduced environmental limitations on food production in Australia and a country in Asia; for example, increased food production due to research into and development of high-yielding and genetically engineered pest resistant varieties, construction of drip irrigation systems, and the use of stubble mulching, intercropping, agroforestry and crop rotation
explaining the impact of the interconnections between environmental, economic and technological factors on the yield of a particular crop, such as wheat, rice or maize, in Australia

AC9HG9K04.minimum_width: Identify at least two environmental challenges to food production in Australia (e.g. soil erosion, salinity, water scarcity) and explain how each reduces productivity; identify at least one management strategy and explain what challenge it addresses.
AC9HG9K04.typical_width: Examine environmental impacts (land and water degradation, salinity, desertification, freshwater shortage, climate change, pollution, competing land uses) causing decline in food production capacity; examine economic and social impacts of competing land uses; examine impacts of biome modifications on First Nations Australians' access to traditional food sources; examine management strategies that improve food security and restore agricultural quality and diversity; generate ideas for strategies to expand production sustainably.
wider: Investigate a specific First Nations food source (e.g. myrrnong/yam daisy in Victoria, cycads or bunya nuts in northern Australia) — trace how biome modification reduced its availability and explain the cultural and nutritional significance of this loss

Examine First Nations food sovereignty movements reclaiming access to traditional food sources — explain what 'food security' means in a First Nations context compared with mainstream food security frameworks
Develop a bush food commercialisation strategy — identify what would be required (land access, market development, knowledge partnerships) and evaluate its food security and ecological sustainability

Evaluate whether a named management strategy (e.g. Landcare revegetation, soil carbon programs) addresses the root cause or the symptom of a food production challenge — explain the ecological mechanisms involved
elaborations: examining environmental impacts of changes to food production causing a decline in the capacity of the land to provide agricultural products; for example, land and water degradation such as soil erosion, salinity and desertification, shortage of fresh water, competing land uses, climate change and pollution contribute to a decrease in food production
examining economic and social impacts of changes to food production; for example, competing land uses such as urban and industrial uses, and recreation activities

examining the impacts of modifications to biomes on the productivity and availability of staple resources for First Nations Australians; for example, reduced access to bush food such as myrrnong (yam daisy) in Victoria or cycads, bunya nuts and wongi plums in northern Australia
examining management strategies that improve food security; for example, efforts to reduce food wastage, government policies or trade barriers

explaining management strategies that restore the quality or diversity of agriculture in Australia; for example, improving the function of natural biomes and anthropogenic biomes, monitoring land management practices, improving the condition of the soil or building the capability of farmers

generating ideas for a strategy to expand agricultural production in Australia; for example, market bush food such as herbs and wattle seed, invest in research, support farm innovations or develop the expertise of farmers

AC9HG9K05.minimum_width: Identify how transport access affects connection to at least two types of services; trace a product through at least three supply chain steps; identify that internet access varies between and within countries and explain at least one consequence.
AC9HG9K05.typical_width: Discuss how transport access shapes perceptions and use of services for people in different locations; explain how transport and information networks function across supply chains from production to consumer including logistics; discuss how communications infrastructure supports collaboration for diverse communities; interpret differences in internet access between and within countries including rural Australia and an Asian country; examine how technologies have enabled places to provide global business services such as call centres in India and the Philippines.
wider: Discuss how communications infrastructure enables Indigenous and marginalised communities (e.g. Masai in Kenya, Inuit in Greenland, Yanomami in Amazon, First Nations Australians in remote communities) to maintain cultural connections across geographic distances

Analyse how mobile-first internet access has become a bridging technology in low-income countries — explain how mobile penetration outpaces fixed broadband across parts of Asia and what this means for connectivity equity
Examine how e-commerce platforms (e.g. Etsy, Amazon) have changed the geographic reach of local producers — trace how supply chain logistics have shifted as a result
Investigate how time zone differences interact with digital technology to enable 24-hour global business service operations — analyse which places are advantaged and disadvantaged by this geography
elaborations: discussing how access to transportation affects the ways people perceive, use and are connected to specific services or opportunities in a place; for example, regional flights to travel to capital cities and to international destinations

identifying and describing how transport and information networks function to connect people to goods and services (for example, from cotton crop to t-shirts or from farm to table), including how supply-chain logistics influence these connections

discussing how communications infrastructure and networks support people to collaborate; for example, local people working for social sustainability and inclusion such as the Masai in Kenya, Berber in North Africa, San or Kalahari Bushmen in southern Africa, Uyghurs in China, Ainu in Japan, Inuit in Greenland and Yanomami in the Amazon Basin

interpreting differences in people's access to the internet between and within countries, such as in rural areas across Australia and across the world, including a country of Asia, and explaining how technologies are used to connect people to information, services and other people
examining how technologies have made it possible for places to provide a range of global business services, such as businesses operating call centres in India and the Philippines

AC9HG9K06.minimum_width: Identify at least three causes of global tourism growth; explain at least one environmental, one economic and one social impact of tourism on a named place; identify one management strategy and explain what impact it addresses.
AC9HG9K06.typical_width: Discuss causes of global tourism growth and its environmental, economic and social impacts on places; explain impacts of cultural and leisure choices on sustainability of tourist places and predict how space tourism or post-COVID recovery may affect places; examine how management plans for national parks such as Uluru-Kata Tjuta integrate cultural and scientific knowledge and experience to manage tourism effects.
wider: Examine pilgrimage tourism (e.g. Mecca, Vatican City, Varanasi) as a distinct case — explain how religious tourism produces different environmental, economic and social impact profiles compared with mass leisure tourism

Investigate the history of the Uluru climbing ban — examine how past governance failures shaped the current co-management approach integrating Anangu cultural authority with scientific land management
Predict how space tourism could affect near-Earth orbital environments — extend the environmental impact framework to a context with no existing management model
Analyse how overtourism affects a specific place — identify which impacts are reversible and which are not, and evaluate what management approaches address each type
elaborations: discussing the causes of the global growth of tourism and its environmental, economic or social impacts on places

explaining the impacts of people's cultural and leisure choices on the sustainability of places popular with tourists (for example, visiting Mecca, Vatican City or Varanasi as religious pilgrimages) and predicting how space tourism or the impacts of COVID-19 may affect places

examining how management plans for national parks, such as Uluru-Kata Tjuta National Park, bring together cultural and scientific knowledge and experience, and examining governance and past experience to manage the effects of people's cultural and leisure choices

AC9HG9K07.minimum_width: Identify products or services that local businesses sell to and buy from other places; explain how and why places are interconnected through trade at at least two scales (local, national or global).
AC9HG9K07.typical_width: Discuss products and services that local businesses sell to or buy from other places; examine how and why places are interconnected nationally, regionally and globally through trade in goods and services; identify examples of change in trade interconnections between places and people over time at local, national and global scales.
wider: Trace how a specific Australian trade relationship (e.g. Australia–China trade in resources or agricultural products) has changed over time — explain what drove the change and how it affected both places
Examine regional trade agreements (e.g. ASEAN, Pacific trade frameworks) — explain how agreements shape the geography of trade interconnections and which places gain or lose
Investigate the role of global cities as trade hubs (e.g. Singapore, Hong Kong) — explain how geographic location and infrastructure concentrate trade interconnections in specific places
Examine how COVID-19 supply chain disruptions altered trade interconnections at local, national and global scales — identify what changes were temporary and what appear to be structural shifts
elaborations: discussing some of the products and/or services that businesses in their local area sell to or buy from other places
examining how and why places are interconnected nationally, regionally and globally through trade in goods and services
identifying examples of change in interconnections between places and people through trade in goods and/or services over time at the local, national and global scale

AC9HG9K08.minimum_width: Explain the environmental, economic or social effects of at least one production type on a place; trace at least three stages of a product supply chain and identify an effect at each stage.
AC9HG9K08.typical_width: Examine the effects on people, places and environments of mining, farming, forestry or manufactured goods production; explain the environmental effects of production and distribution of consumer products on places throughout the supply chain including the e-waste chain; evaluate the environmental, economic and social impacts of the global oil supply chain from extraction to waste disposal in Australia and West Asia; examine a government waste management strategy and identify sustainability implications.
wider: Analyse the geographic asymmetry of supply chain impacts — map which countries bear extraction environmental costs and which bear waste costs, and explain why this distribution persists

Investigate the concept of externalities applied to a supply chain — explain why environmental costs are often borne by places different from those that capture economic benefits, and what policy interventions attempt to address this
Examine extended producer responsibility policies — explain how shifting waste management costs back to producers changes the supply chain logic and what sustainability outcomes result

Compare the impacts of oil extraction and oil consumption across West Asian and Australian contexts — explain who bears environmental costs and who captures economic benefits, and evaluate current management strategies for each
elaborations: examining the effects on people, places or environments of mining, farming, forestry or the production of manufactured goods

explaining the environmental effects of the production and distribution of consumer products and services on the places that produce the raw materials, the people who make the products, and the environments that receive the waste at the end of the products' life; for example, the environmental effects of an e-waste supply chain from mining, production and sales to waste disposal

evaluating the environmental, economic and social impacts of the global oil supply chain, from where the resource is extracted, processed and sold, and how impacts could be sustainably managed in Australia and in West Asia

examining a strategy used by local, state or national governments to manage waste in one of Australia's cities or regional urban centres, and identifying implications for sustainability (environmental, economic and social factors)

AC9HG9S01.minimum_width: Develop at least three open, investigable questions that address a geographical phenomenon or challenge from different angles (causes, impacts, connections or management); modify at least one question to incorporate a geographical concept or scale specification.
AC9HG9S01.typical_width: Develop a range of questions to investigate why a geographical phenomenon has changed or a challenge may arise; develop and modify questions using geographical concepts and scale to sharpen inquiry focus; plan an investigation of a biome or connections topic at a range of scales using digital tools.
wider: Develop inquiry questions for two different topic contexts (biomes and interconnections) — compare how the same question types operate differently across these phenomena
Evaluate two possible investigation plans for the same sharpened question — explain which is more feasible and would produce better geographical data, using scale and tool-appropriateness criteria
Design a multi-scale investigation plan specifying different digital tools for different scales — explain why each tool is appropriate for its scale and question type
Develop a question sequence that structures an inquiry from broad phenomenon to specific researchable focus — explain the logical progression from opening question to driving research question
elaborations: developing a range of questions to investigate why a geographical phenomenon has changed or why a challenge may arise; for example, 'Why is food security important?', 'What are sources of food in Australia?', 'How are people, places and environments connected?'

developing and modifying questions to sharpen the focus of an investigation using concepts or scale of study; for example, 'Why is the security and sustainability of food production important at the national scale?', 'How can bush food become a sustainable nutritional source of food in Australia?', 'How can connections between people, environments and places affect the sustainability of places at the global scale?'

planning an investigation of a geographical phenomenon or challenge being studied at a range of scales, using digital tools; for example, the diverse types of biomes modified by humans for food and non-food products at a national and global scale, or the different types of connections between people and places at local, national and global scales

AC9HG9S02.minimum_width: Identify at least two primary research methods and collect at least two secondary sources using targeted criteria; evaluate each source for relevance and reliability; create one multi-variable data representation; construct a map with at least four cartographic conventions.
AC9HG9S02.typical_width: Identify primary research methods including fieldwork to collect original materials; collect relevant secondary research materials online using targeted criteria and evaluate for relevance and reliability; create presentations and visual representations of multi-variable geographical data using digital tools (tables, complex graphs, diagrams, cross-sections); represent spatial distributions by constructing special purpose maps conforming to cartographic conventions.
wider: Construct a map using GIS software — explain how digital tools change the map construction process and what spatial analysis they enable that manual maps cannot

Develop a source evaluation rubric for a geography inquiry — specify criteria and weightings for relevance and reliability, and apply it to a set of sources spanning government, news and peer-reviewed types
Create a 3D diagram or flow diagram showing process interactions (e.g. oil spill impacts on aquatic food production) — explain why a 2D representation would be insufficient for the phenomenon
Evaluate a published data visualisation for what it communicates well and what it obscures — explain how the choice of representation type affects what relationships are visible
elaborations: identifying primary research methods, including fieldwork, to collect original materials; for example, comparison of aerial photographs or field sketches over time to document the use or alteration of biomes by people, or surveying peers on their use of the internet or other technologies

collecting relevant secondary research materials online using targeted criteria; for example, "connections between food security and deforestation in Bangladesh", "the digital divide and its impacts on people and places in North Korea"

evaluating primary or secondary research materials for relevance (for example, "Does the information reflect current thinking on sustainable food production?") and reliability (for example, "Who is/are the author/s? Does the author reference other experts or reports in the field of environmental management?")

creating a presentation of data and information using geospatial technologies; for example, a 3D diagram illustrating interactions between an oil spill in coral reefs and resultant decline in aquatic food production; a flow diagram showing the daily activities of a female subsistence farmer in Africa; or a diagram of a mangrove ecosystem before and after human interactions

creating visual representations of multi-variable geographical data using digital tools; for example, a table to compare the daily consumption of meat per person in developed and developing countries; a complex graph to illustrate the relationship between temperature, precipitation and biomes; or a cross-section identifying horizons in a soil profile, and the impacts of mining and fracking on agricultural land

representing spatial distribution of geographical phenomena by constructing special purpose maps that conform to cartographic conventions, for example creating a map to show the relationship between biomes and world food production

AC9HG9S03.minimum_width: Make at least one generalisation supported by evidence from a dataset; identify at least one pattern or trend in geographical data and explain it with reference to a geographical factor; identify at least one causal relationship between variables in data.
AC9HG9S03.typical_width: Make generalisations about trends using questionnaires, interviews or quantitative datasets; explain patterns using current indices and data sources (e.g. Global Hunger Index, Food and Agricultural Organization data, transport network maps with survey responses); explain relationships between causes and impacts of factors including GPS/GIS technology effects on farming or tourism transport choices.
wider: Compare generalisations made from qualitative sources (interviews, surveys) with those from quantitative sources (statistics, indices) about the same geographical phenomenon — explain what each type of data reveals and what it cannot
Identify a relationship in the data that could be correlation rather than causation — explain what additional evidence would be needed to establish causation and design how it could be collected

Trace a multi-step causal chain in geographical data (e.g. technology adoption → precision farming → reduced run-off → sustained productivity) — explain each causal link and identify where the chain could break
Analyse unexpected features in a pattern — identify what additional factor or exception the data reveals beyond the main trend, and explain what this means for the generalisation
elaborations: making generalisations about trends; for example, using questionnaires or interviews to identify people's perspectives on live food fish trade in Australia or people's access to the internet in the local area

explaining a pattern; for example, using the current Global Hunger Index and the updated Food and Agricultural Organization's Low-Income Food-Deficit Countries (LIFDCs) to identify locations of food scarcity and malnutrition, or comparing maps showing transport networks with survey responses on personal mobility

explaining relationships between causes and impacts of factors represented in data; for example, the impact of the use of Global Positioning System (GPS) and Geographic Information Systems (GIS) on the way farmers control the dispersion of fertilisers and pesticides to produce higher yields and limit run-off, or the effects of the use of GPS to construct maps on how tourists use different transport systems to visits popular places in Australia

AC9HG9S04.minimum_width: Draw at least one conclusion about the impact of a geographical challenge, supported by specific evidence; identify at least two perspectives on the challenge and explain the reasons for each.
AC9HG9S04.typical_width: Draw conclusions about the impact of a geographical challenge on people, places and environments from multiple data sources; justify conclusions by reflecting on environmental, economic and social perspectives identified and the reasons for these perspectives, for example considering impacts of disappearing arable land or ecotourism.
wider: Identify a case where two perspectives on the same challenge produce contradictory conclusions — explain how to acknowledge or resolve the contradiction within a justified conclusion

Reflect on how your own geographic position as an Australian student shapes what data is accessible and what conclusions feel obvious — identify whose perspectives are harder to access from this position
Evaluate a published geographical conclusion — identify whose perspectives are represented and whose are absent, and explain how this affects the conclusion's validity and scope
Draw conclusions at two different scales for the same geographical challenge — explain how the conclusion changes as scale changes and what this means for the conclusions' applicability
elaborations: drawing conclusions about the impact of a geographical challenge on people, places and environments; for example, investigating the causes of a decline in food species, its impacts on food security and the establishment of the Svalbard Global Seed Vault, or the effects of cyberattacks on technological interconnections and implementation of international laws related to cyber security

justifying conclusions by reflecting on perspectives identified and reasons for these perspectives; for example, considering environmental, economic and social factors when challenging disappearing arable land converted from food production to non-food crops, or promoting ecotourism that impacts on people and places

AC9HG9S05.minimum_width: Propose at least one individual and one collective strategy for a geographical challenge with reasons; evaluate one strategy against at least two of the three criteria (environmental, economic, social); recommend a strategy and explain at least two predicted impacts.
AC9HG9S05.typical_width: Propose individual actions (e.g. reducing food wastage, reducing tourist impact) and collective actions (e.g. food security organisations, improving labour practices) with supporting reasons; evaluate effectiveness of strategies against environmental, economic and social criteria; explain outcomes and impacts of a strategy; reflect on the influence of personal values and attitudes on predicted outcomes.
wider: Identify trade-offs in a strategy evaluation — explain where a strategy performs well against one criterion while performing poorly against another, and explain what this means for the recommendation
Produce a recommendation that addresses likely counterarguments — explain why the recommendation stands despite limitations identified in the evaluation
Reflect on how values embedded in a government or organisational strategy differ from personal values — explain what this reveals about whose interests are prioritised in the strategy design
Compare the scale of impact of individual versus collective strategies for the same challenge — explain what individual action cannot achieve alone and what collective action requires to succeed
elaborations: proposing individual action and supporting the proposal with reasons; for example, reducing food wastage or reducing negative environmental impacts when visiting theme parks or national parks

proposing collective action and supporting the proposal with reasons; for example, organisations that work to end hunger and improve food security, or improve labour practices and increase wages for people working to produce goods exported to other countries

evaluating the effectiveness of a strategy in relation to environmental, economic or social criteria; for example, examining factors likely to impact on achieving Goal 2 of the Sustainable Development Goals – Ending global hunger by 2030 or monitoring the extent that a management plan for a national park is implemented

explaining the outcomes and impacts of a strategy, such as providing people with adequate and quality food that is acceptable in different cultures, or reducing the global movement of hazardous waste between countries

reflecting on the influence of personal values and attitudes on predicted outcomes and impacts; for example, how preferring to buy locally produced food reduces food miles and greenhouse gases, or how reducing, recycling and reusing goods contributes to a more sustainable environment

AC9HG9S06.minimum_width: Use at least three geographical concepts and five geographical terms correctly in a response; incorporate at least one data representation and reference at least one research finding with acknowledgement; apply a consistent tone appropriate to an identified audience.
AC9HG9S06.typical_width: Develop responses using geographical concepts and terms; create descriptions using maps, photographs, diagrams, graphs, tables or satellite images as evidence and incorporating and acknowledging research findings; create explanations applying audience-appropriate tone and reasoned argument — for example, strategies to improve sustainability of a place or environment, or a management plan for a tourist hotspot.
wider: Produce two versions of the same response for different audiences — explain how tone, vocabulary and structural choices differ and why, maintaining the same geographical knowledge base
Evaluate a published geographical response for tone-audience fit — identify where tone choices strengthen or undermine the argument and what revision would improve it

Use two related geographical concepts together in a single explanation (e.g. scale and interconnection; environment and sustainability) — explain how using them together produces a richer analysis than using each independently

Construct a response where the structure is driven by research findings rather than a predetermined argument — explain how the evidence shapes the response structure rather than being inserted to support a pre-formed conclusion
elaborations: developing a response using geographical concepts and terms; for example, strategies to improve the sustainability of a place or environment

creating a description, using representations of data (for example, using maps to illustrate the major terrestrial biomes of Australia and photographs to show their impacts on people and places) and research findings (for example, using diagrams, graphs, tables and/or satellite images to show how environmental, economic or technological factors affect crop yields)

creating an explanation that applies tone appropriate to the audience; such as reducing food wastage, or developing a management plan for a tourist hot spot, in an authoritative tone and reasoned argument
